claim: Dopamine converts hippocampal spike timing-dependent depression into potentiation during continued synaptic activity.
source: Previously, we reported that the reinforcement signal dopamine converts hippocampal spike timing-dependent depression into potentiation during continued synaptic activity (Brzosko et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Brzosko et al., 2015).

claim: Postsynaptic bursts in the presence of dopamine produce input-specific LTP in mouse hippocampal synapses 10 min after they were primed with coincident pre- and post-synaptic activity (post-before-pre pairing; Δt = –20 ms).
source: Here, we report that postsynaptic bursts in the presence of dopamine produce input-specific LTP in mouse hippocampal synapses 10 min after they were primed with coincident pre- and post-synaptic activity (post-before-pre pairing; Δt = –20 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figures 1D and 1F.

claim: The priming activity induces synaptic depression and sets an NMDA receptor-dependent silent eligibility trace.
source: This priming activity induces synaptic depression and sets an NMDA receptor-dependent silent eligibility trace which, through the cAMP-PKA cascade, is rapidly converted into protein synthesis-dependent synaptic potentiation, mediated by a signaling pathway distinct from that of conventional LTP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that NMDAR antagonists block the eligibility trace (Figure 2D, 2E, 2F).

claim: The eligibility trace is converted into protein synthesis-dependent synaptic potentiation through the cAMP-PKA cascade.
source: This priming activity induces synaptic depression and sets an NMDA receptor-dependent silent eligibility trace which, through the cAMP-PKA cascade, is rapidly converted into protein synthesis-dependent synaptic potentiation, mediated by a signaling pathway distinct from that of conventional LTP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing involvement of AC1/AC8 (Figure 4B), PKA (Figure 4C), and protein synthesis (Figure 5A).

claim: The synaptic potentiation is mediated by a signaling pathway distinct from that of conventional LTP.
source: This priming activity induces synaptic depression and sets an NMDA receptor-dependent silent eligibility trace which, through the cAMP-PKA cascade, is rapidly converted into protein synthesis-dependent synaptic potentiation, mediated by a signaling pathway distinct from that of conventional LTP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that conventional t-LTP does not require AC1/AC8 (Figure 4B), PKA (Figure 4C), or protein synthesis (Figure 5A), while reactivation-induced LTP does.

claim: The reactivation-induced plasticity mechanism adds specificity to reinforcement learning by controlling memory allocation.
source: This synaptic learning rule was incorporated into a computational model, and we found that it adds specificity to reinforcement learning by controlling memory allocation and enabling both 'instructive' and 'supervised' reinforcement learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The reactivation-induced plasticity mechanism enables both 'instructive' and 'supervised' reinforcement learning.
source: This synaptic learning rule was incorporated into a computational model, and we found that it adds specificity to reinforcement learning by controlling memory allocation and enabling both 'instructive' and 'supervised' reinforcement learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Reactivated neurons activate more strongly than non-reactivated cells in freely moving mice performing a reward-based navigation task.
source: We predicted that this mechanism would make reactivated neurons activate more strongly and carry more spatial information than non-reactivated cells, which was confirmed in freely moving mice performing a reward-based navigation task.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8D and 8F.

claim: Reactivated neurons carry more spatial information than non-reactivated cells in freely moving mice performing a reward-based navigation task.
source: We predicted that this mechanism would make reactivated neurons activate more strongly and carry more spatial information than non-reactivated cells, which was confirmed in freely moving mice performing a reward-based navigation task.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Post-before-pre pairing protocol (Δt = –20 ms) leads to input-specific synaptic depression (t-LTD).
source: Single postsynaptic action potentials followed by presynaptic input stimulation (post-before-pre protocol, Δt = –20 ms) led to input-specific synaptic depression in the test pathway (t-LTD; 61% ± 11% vs 100%, t(9) = 3.7, p=0.005, n=10; Figure 1B and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Application of DA alone, without resuming synaptic stimulation after the pairing protocol, does not affect the depression.
source: Application of DA alone, without resuming synaptic stimulation after this pairing protocol, did not affect the depression (53% ± 7% vs 100%, t(5) = 7.0, p=0.0009, n=6; Figure 1C and F blue trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Postsynaptic action potential bursts (5–6 APs) in the presence of DA, 10 min after the pairing protocol, trigger an immediate induction of synaptic potentiation.
source: Strikingly, postsynaptic action potential bursts (5–6 APs) in the presence of DA, 10 min after the pairing protocol, triggered an immediate induction of synaptic potentiation (135% ± 14.9% vs 100%, t(8) = 2.4, p=0.044, n=9; Figure 1D and F red trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Burst stimulation alone, in the absence of DA, does not prevent synaptic depression.
source: Burst stimulation alone, in the absence of DA, did not prevent synaptic depression (72% ± 12% vs 100%, t(6) = 2.5, p=0.048, n=7; Figure 1E and F black trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The pairing protocol sets an eligibility trace allowing activated synapses to be selectively altered minutes later by reactivation of the postsynaptic neuron in the presence of DA.
source: This result suggests that the pairing protocol sets an eligibility trace allowing activated synapses to be selectively altered minutes later by reactivation of the postsynaptic neuron in the presence of DA.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental results showing that burst+DA induces potentiation only after prior pairing.

claim: These are the longest-lasting synaptic eligibility traces reported in the brain.
source: To our knowledge, these are the longest-lasting synaptic eligibility traces reported in the brain.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with existing literature and the 10-minute delay observed in the experiments.

claim: Synaptic potentiation is not observed without prior spike pairing.
source: First, we found that synaptic potentiation was indeed not observed without prior spike pairing (93% ± 8% vs 100%, t(6) = 0.84, p=0.43, n=7; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Induction of hippocampal t-LTD requires metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs).
source: Induction of hippocampal t-LTD requires metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs; Andrade-Talavera et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The mGluR antagonist MPEP blocks t-LTD.
source: This blocked t-LTD (94% ± 6% vs 100%, t(6) = 0.95, p=0.38, n=7; Figure 2B and C, blue; vs control t-LTD 69% ± 7%, n=7; t(11.5) = 2.67, p=0.02; Figure 2B and C, black)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: MPEP does not block burst-induced potentiation.
source: but burst-induced potentiation was intact (131% ± 10% vs 100%, t(6) = 3.07, p=0.021, n=7; Figure 2B and C, red)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Setting the eligibility trace by spike pairing is distinct from the signaling mechanism that mediates t-LTD.
source: suggesting that setting the eligibility trace by spike pairing is distinct from the signaling mechanism that mediates t-LTD.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the dissociation between t-LTD (blocked by MPEP) and eligibility trace (not blocked by MPEP).

claim: Application of the NMDAR antagonist d-AP5 during pairing (Δt = –20 ms) abolishes both t-LTD and the subsequent burst-induced potentiation.
source: We found that application of the NMDAR antagonist d-AP5 during pairing (Δt = –20 ms) abolished both t-LTD and the subsequent burst-induced potentiation, resulting in no change of synaptic weights (100% ± 9% vs 100%, t(6) = 0.043, p=0.97, n=7; Figure 2D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Loading the postsynaptic cell with the NMDAR channel blocker MK801 through the recording pipette does not affect t-LTD.
source: Loading the postsynaptic cell with the NMDAR channel blocker MK801 through the recording pipette did not affect t-LTD (68% ± 7% vs 100%, t(5) = 4.77, p=0.005, n=6; Figure 2E and F)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Postsynaptic MK801 completely abolishes burst-induced potentiation, leaving synaptic depression instead.
source: but completely abolished burst-induced potentiation, leaving synaptic depression instead (61% ± 10% vs 100%, t(6) = 3.85, p=0.0084, n=6; Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a double dissociation between t-LTD induced by mGluR and non-postsynaptic NMDAR signaling and the eligibility trace for reactivation-induced potentiation set by postsynaptic ionotropic NMDARs.
source: These results show a double dissociation between t-LTD induced by mGluR and non-postsynaptic NMDAR signaling and the eligibility trace for reactivation-induced potentiation set by postsynaptic ionotropic NMDARs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the differential effects of MPEP and postsynaptic MK801 on t-LTD versus eligibility trace.

claim: The NMDAR antagonist d-AP5, applied after the pairing protocol but before burst stimulation, does not affect burst-induced potentiation.
source: However, the NMDAR antagonist d-AP5, applied after the pairing protocol but before burst stimulation, did not affect burst-induced potentiation (127% ± 9%, t(5) = 2.94, p=0.032, n=6; Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Application of nimodipine, an L-type VGCC blocker, before the burst completely abolishes LTP and leaves synaptic depression instead.
source: In contrast, voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) are required as application of nimodipine, an L-type VGCC blocker, before the burst completely abolished LTP and left synaptic depression instead (72% ± 5% vs 100%, t(5) = 5.6, p=0.0026, n=6; Figure 3B and C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Ca2+ entry through VGCCs is required for burst reactivation to induce LTP.
source: indicating that, as in some other forms of synaptic potentiation (Grover and Teyler, 1990), Ca2+ entry through VGCCs is required for burst reactivation to induce LTP.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the nimodipine experiment and is supported by citation to similar findings.

claim: Coincident DA signaling and postsynaptic Ca2+ increase enable the potentiation of previously primed synapses.
source: These findings suggest that coincident DA signaling and postsynaptic Ca2+ increase enable the potentiation of previously primed synapses.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the requirement of both DA and Ca2+ (through VGCCs) for burst-induced potentiation.

claim: Adenylyl cyclases (ACs) are activated by Gs-coupled dopamine D1/D5 receptor stimulation.
source: They are activated by Gs-coupled dopamine D1/D5 receptor stimulation (Neve et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: AC subtypes AC1 and AC8 are additionally Ca2+-stimulated.
source: and subtypes AC1 and AC8 are additionally Ca2+- stimulated (Wayman et al., 1994; Watson et al., 2000; Ferguson and Storm, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In AC1/AC8 double knockout (AC DKO) mice, the conversion to potentiation by burst stimulation in the presence of DA after a negative pairing protocol is absent.
source: When postsynaptic burst stimulation in the presence of DA was applied after a negative pairing protocol (Δt = –20 ms; Figure 4Ai) in slices from AC DKO mice, the conversion to potentiation was absent and significantly different from DA- and burst-induced potentiation in slices from wildtype mice (AC DKO, 90% ± 8%, n=6 vs WT, 132% ± 11%, n=8; t(12) = 2.8, p=0.015; Figure 4Bi and Biii)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: AC1/AC8 acts as a coincidence detector for DA- and Ca2+-induced potentiation.
source: revealing a role for AC1/AC8 as coincidence detector for DA- and Ca2+-induced potentiation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the requirement of AC1/AC8 for burst-induced potentiation.

claim: Conventional, DA-independent t-LTP induced by a pre-before-post pairing protocol (Δt = +10 ms) shows significant potentiation comparable to that seen in wildtype mice in AC DKO mice.
source: In contrast, conventional, DA-independent t-LTP induced by a pre-before-post pairing protocol (Δt = +10 ms; Figure 4Aii) showed significant potentiation comparable to that seen in wildtype mice (AC DKO, 150% ± 19% vs 100%, t(5) = 2.6, p=0.049, n=6; WT, 163% ± 14% vs 100%, t(9) = 4.4, p=0.0015, n=10; Figure 4Bii and Biii).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: AC activation produces an increase in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) which activates protein kinase A (PKA).
source: AC activation produces an increase in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) which activates protein kinase A (PKA; Sassone-Corsi, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Loading the postsynaptic cell with a PKA blocker, protein kinase inhibitor-(6-22)-amide, through the recording pipette prevents burst-induced potentiation in the presence of DA after the post-before-pre protocol.
source: In this configuration burst stimulation in the presence of DA after the post-before-pre protocol failed to induce synaptic potentiation (69% ± 13% vs 100%, t(5) = 2.4, p=0.064, n=6; Figure 4Ci and Ciii).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Conventional pre-before-post pairing induces significant potentiation in the presence of postsynaptic PKA blocker, albeit of somewhat reduced magnitude.
source: In contrast, conventional pre-before-post pairing induced significant potentiation, albeit of somewhat reduced magnitude (137% ± 14% vs 100%, t(5) = 2.63, p=0.0463, n=6; Figure 4Cii and Ciii).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The requirement of DA and PKA for burst-induced potentiation is shared with late-phase LTP.
source: The requirement of DA and PKA for burst-induced potentiation is shared with late-phase LTP (Frey et al., 1990; Frey et al., 1993), which requires protein synthesis (Frey et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Late-phase LTP requires protein synthesis.
source: The requirement of DA and PKA for burst-induced potentiation is shared with late-phase LTP (Frey et al., 1990; Frey et al., 1993), which requires protein synthesis (Frey et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: With anisomycin delivered to the postsynaptic cell through the recording pipette, burst stimulation in the presence of DA no longer induces conversion to potentiation but leaves a synaptic depression instead.
source: We found that, with anisomycin, burst stimulation in the presence of DA no longer induced conversion to potentiation but left a synaptic depression instead, which was significantly different from vehicle control (AM, 52% ± 11% vs 100%, t(5) = 4.5, p=0.0062, n=6; Figure 5Ai and Aiii, red; vs vehicle, 128% ± 17%, n=5; t(9) = 3.9, p=0.0033; Figure 5Ai and Aiii, green).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Conventional t-LTP induced by pre-before-post pairing is unaffected by anisomycin.
source: In contrast, conventional t-LTP induced by pre-before-post pairing was unaffected by anisomycin (161% ± 20% vs 100%, t(5) = 3.0, p=0.029, n=6; Figure 5Aii and Aiii, black).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The post-before-pre pairing protocol induces t-LTD in the presence of postsynaptic anisomycin.
source: Furthermore, the post-before-pre pairing protocol induced t-LTD under these conditions (65% ± 6% vs 100%, t(5) = 5.9, p=0.0019, n=6; Figure 5Aii and Aiii, gray).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Postsynaptically applied anisomycin does not affect synaptic responses in baseline conditions.
source: We confirmed that postsynaptically applied anisomycin did not affect synaptic responses in baseline conditions (95% ± 9.7% vs 100%, t(6) = 0.56, p=0.59, n=7; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Spike amplitude during pairing in cells with anisomycin shows no significant difference compared to cells loaded with vehicle controls.
source: Spike amplitude (AM 112 mV ± 3 mV, Vehicle 111 mV ± 3 mV) and spike width (AM 3.3 ms ± 0.2 ms, Vehicle 3.3 ms ± 0.2 ms) showed no significant differences (amplitude t(10) = 0.09050, p=0.92; width t(10) = 0.1134, p=0.91; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Spike width during pairing in cells with anisomycin shows no significant difference compared to cells loaded with vehicle controls.
source: Spike amplitude (AM 112 mV ± 3 mV, Vehicle 111 mV ± 3 mV) and spike width (AM 3.3 ms ± 0.2 ms, Vehicle 3.3 ms ± 0.2 ms) showed no significant differences (amplitude t(10) = 0.09050, p=0.92; width t(10) = 0.1134, p=0.91; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: After a priming event, burst reactivation in the presence of DA induces a rapid form of protein synthesis-dependent LTP.
source: These experimental results show that, after a priming event, burst reactivation in the presence of DA induces a rapid form of protein synthesis-dependent LTP.
evidence: This claim is a summary inference based on the experimental results presented.

claim: The reactivation-induced plasticity mechanism ensures that only salient neuronal activity induces long-term changes in the network.
source: This mechanism would ensure that only salient neuronal activity induces long-term changes in the network.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the functional implications of the mechanism.

claim: When using a standard reinforcement learning (RL) rule, which does not depend on burst reactivation, all previously primed synapses are potentiated after receiving the DA signal.
source: When using a standard reinforcement learning (RL) rule, which does not depend on burst reactivation, all previously primed synapses are potentiated after receiving the DA signal (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When applying the burst-dependent learning rule, in which potentiation of primed synapses depends on both the reward signal and reactivation, a selected subset of inputs becomes potentiated, while inputs on non-reactivated neurons remain depressed.
source: In contrast, when applying the burst-dependent learning rule (Equation 1) to the network, in which potentiation of primed synapses depends on both the reward signal and reactivation, a selected subset of inputs becomes potentiated, while inputs on non-reactivated neurons remain depressed (gray) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The most excitable cells would be the most likely to show action potential bursts during reactivation and, therefore, show synaptic potentiation according to the memory allocation hypothesis.
source: According to this scenario, the most excitable cells would be the most likely to show action potential bursts during reactivation and, therefore, show synaptic potentiation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the memory allocation hypothesis cited in the text.

claim: There is evidence for replay of prioritized experience.
source: Alternatively, there is evidence for replay of prioritized experience (Igata et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cells encoding the most salient events preceding the reward would reactivate, and thereby determine which set of cells would show potentiation during reward.
source: suggesting that cells encoding the most salient events preceding the reward would reactivate, and thereby determine which set of cells would show potentiation during reward (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the prioritized experience hypothesis.

claim: The exclusive requirement of postsynaptic activity for potentiation to occur offers the possibility that other inputs active at the reward location carry additional information about the nature of the reward or the reward location, which could elicit postsynaptic bursting activity.
source: In addition, because of the exclusive requirement of postsynaptic activity for potentiation to occur, this mechanism offers another intriguing possibility, namely that other inputs active at the reward location carries additional information about the nature of the reward, e.g., food, or the reward location, such as the presence of specific landmarks, which could elicit postsynaptic bursting activity.
evidence: This claim is speculation about possible functional implications of the mechanism.

claim: When different instructive inputs induce bursting each in distinct subsets of neurons during reward, selective increases in synaptic weights would not only enable the encoding of reward but also distinguish between different rewards.
source: When different instructive inputs induce bursting each in distinct subsets of neurons during reward, selective increases in synaptic weights would not only enable the encoding of reward but also distinguish between different rewards (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The burst-dependent learning rule enables the network to selectively learn relevant information by allowing feedback input to assign which part of the network is responding.
source: By allowing feedback input to assign which part of the network is responding, the burst-dependent learning rule enables the network to selectively learn relevant information (Figure 7B)
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The burst-dependent learning rule results in potentiation of those synapses that are active temporally separated, but less when simultaneously active.
source: resulting in potentiation of those synapses (magenta and cyan in Figure 7Biii) that are active temporally separated, but less when simultaneous active (Figure 7Biv).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7Biii and 7Biv.

claim: The burst-dependent learning rule provides a mechanism to associate temporally separated, reward-relevant information in a neuronal network.
source: This provides a mechanism to associate temporally separated, reward-relevant information in a neuronal network.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: The burst-dependent learning rule provides the network with a gating mechanism for memory allocation to an engram.
source: The burst-dependent learning rule provides the network with a gating mechanism for memory allocation to an engram.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: Burst-induced plasticity reduces the number of neurons encoding the reward location and other reward-related information, increasing the specificity of synaptic memory in a neuronal network.
source: Thus, burst-induced plasticity reduces the number of neurons encoding the reward location and other reward-related information, increasing the specificity of synaptic memory in a neuronal network.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: When an animal navigates toward a reward, the previously reactivated hippocampal neurons would be more strongly activated than non-reactivated neurons.
source: Based on these results we predicted that, when an animal navigates toward a reward, the previously reactivated hippocampal neurons would be more strongly activated than non-reactivated neurons.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Of the cells that were active on the maze in a given trial, 44 ± 1% were reactivated at either or both of the reward locations.
source: Of the cells that were active on the maze in a given trial, 44 ± 1% were reactivated at either or both of the reward locations.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data.

claim: There was no detectable difference between the number of cells reactivating at the previously learnt or new reward location.
source: There was no detectable difference between the number of cells reactivating at the previously learnt or new reward location (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: 15 ± 2% of cells reactivated during immobility at non-rewarded locations.
source: Less frequent were the reactivations during immobility at non-rewarded locations where 15 ± 2% of cells reactivated (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Cells with the largest activity peaks during locomotion were the most likely to reactivate at the reward location.
source: Cells with the largest activity peaks during locomotion were the most likely to reactivate at the reward location.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data.

claim: Following their first reactivation, cells had larger activity peaks than the previously non-reactivated cells (0.54 ± 0.01 vs 0.42 ± 0.01 of the cell's max AUC, F(1,16) = 10.12, p=0.006).
source: Following their first reactivation, they had larger activity peaks than the previously non-reactivated cells (0.54 ± 0.01 vs 0.42 ± 0.01 of the cell's max AUC, F(1,16) = 10.12, p=0.006, Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The effect on activity peaks was specific to reward locations, and reactivation at other locations did not affect activity peaks in the following trials (F(1, 16)=0.56, p=0.47).
source: The effect on activity peaks was specific to reward locations, and reactivation at other locations did not affect activity peaks in the following trials (F(1, 16)=0.56, p=0.47, Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The effect of reactivation was independent of the cell event rates.
source: The effect of reactivation was independent of the cell event rates: of two cell groups with matching event rates in a given trial, the one whose cells were reactivated at reward for the first time, had larger peaks in the following trial (F(1, 16)=7.54, p=0.02, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The activity peaks in the trial following the reactivation did not correlate with the time from the activity during locomotion to the reactivation.
source: To test the first, we confirmed that the activity peaks in the trial following the reactivation did not correlate with the time from the activity during locomotion to the reactivation (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8E, suggesting a long-lasting eligibility trace.

claim: The reactivated cells maintained higher calcium activity peaks than non-reactivated cells throughout the later trials.
source: To test the persistence of the change, we confirmed that the reactivated cells maintained higher calcium activity peaks than non-reactivated cells throughout the later trials (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The peaks during locomotion increased in the trial immediately before the first reactivation at reward.
source: Typically, the peaks during locomotion increased in the trial immediately before the first reactivation at reward (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that more excited cells are the ones that undergo the change.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 60% of the reactivated cells (n=971 from 7 mice) and 42% of the non-reactivated cells (n=284 from 7 mice) showed activity at specific locations and were classified as place cells.
source: 60% of the reactivated cells (n=971 from 7 mice) and 42% of the non-reactivated cells (n=284 from 7 mice) showed activity at specific locations and were classified as place cells (see Methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data.

claim: Both place cells and non-place cells showed higher calcium peaks following reactivation and the increase in place cells was not significantly different from that in non-place cells (F(1,16) = 0.11, p=0.75).
source: Both place cells and non-place cells showed higher calcium peaks following reactivation and the increase in place cells was not significantly different from that in non-place cells (F(1,16) = 0.11, p=0.75, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The place map peaks increased significantly more in the place cells that reactivated in trial 4 or later than in the non-reactivated place cells (place map peak ratio 1.4 ± 0.1 vs 1.1 ± 0.1, n=194 reactivated and n=306 non-reactivated place cells; permutation test for repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 16)=11.3, p=0.008).
source: The place map peaks increased significantly more in the place cells that reactivated in trial 4 or later than in the non-reactivated place cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B, place map peak ratio 1.4 ± 0.1 vs 1.1 ± 0.1, n=194 reactivated and n=306 non-reactivated place cells; permutation test for repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 16)=11.3, p=0.008).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The change in spatial information significantly differed between reactivated and non-reactivated place cells (change by 0.011 ± 0.016 to −0.047 ± 0.014 a.u.; permutation test for repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 16)=4.4, p=0.048).
source: The change in spatial information also significantly differed between the two groups (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C, change by 0.011 ± 0.016 to −0.047 ± 0.014 a.u.; permutation test for repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 16)=4.4, p=0.048)
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C.

claim: There was no significant difference in place map stability between reactivated and non-reactivated place cells (correlation of 0.45 ± 0.02 vs 0.47 ± 0.02; permutation test for repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 16)=0.29, p=0.59).
source: but there was no significant difference in place map stability (Figure 8—figure supplement 2E, correlation of 0.45 ± 0.02 vs 0.47 ± 0.02; permutation test for repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 16)=0.29, p=0.59).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The time from the activity during locomotion to the reactivation did not correlate with a change in spatial information.
source: The time from the activity during locomotion to the reactivation did not correlate with a change in spatial information (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Reactivated place cells conveyed more spatial information in late trials (trials 5–8) compared to place cells that did not reactivate (0.15 ± 0.01 vs 0.12 ± 0.01 a.u.; permutation test for repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 16)=4.4, p=0.055).
source: Reactivated place cells conveyed more spatial information in late trials (trials 5–8) compared to place cells that did not reactivate (0.15 ± 0.01 vs 0.12 ± 0.01 a.u.; permutation test for repeated measures ANOVA: F(1, 16)=4.4, p=0.055).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data with statistical analysis.

claim: The learning-associated increase in calcium response and spatial information supports a reactivation-dependent LTP-like mechanism in vivo.
source: This learning-associated increase in calcium response and spatial information supports a reactivation-dependent LTP-like mechanism in vivo (Cacucci et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the in vivo results and is supported by citation to related work.

claim: Postsynaptic burst reactivation of CA1 pyramidal cells in the presence of the reward signal DA rapidly potentiates synapses that have previously undergone a spike timing-dependent priming protocol.
source: We found that postsynaptic burst reactivation of CA1 pyramidal cells in the presence of the reward signal DA rapidly potentiates synapses that have previously undergone a spike timing-dependent priming protocol, providing direct evidence for reactivation-induced synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: Reactivation-induced plasticity is mediated by two sequential coincidence detectors: postsynaptic NMDARs detecting coincident pre- and postsynaptic activity and AC1/AC8 as coincidence detector of DA and reactivation-induced Ca2+ increase.
source: The results suggest that reactivation-induced plasticity is mediated by two sequential coincidence detectors: postsynaptic NMDARs detecting coincident pre- and postsynaptic activity and AC1/AC8 as coincidence detector of DA and reactivation-induced Ca2+ increase.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental results showing requirements for NMDARs and AC1/AC8.

claim: AC1/AC8 is synergistically activated when the two signals, Gs-coupled dopamine D1/D5 receptor activation and Ca2+ influx, occur at the same time.
source: AC1/AC8 is synergistically activated when the two signals, Gs-coupled dopamine D1/D5 receptor activation and Ca2+ influx, occur at the same time (Wayman et al., 1994; Watson et al., 2000; Ferguson and Storm, 2004; Neve et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Burst pairing, but not pairings of single pre- and postsynaptic action potentials, induces synaptic plasticity at 1.3 mM extracellular calcium in rat hippocampal slices.
source: It was recently reported that burst pairing, but not pairings of single pre- and postsynaptic action potentials, induces synaptic plasticity at 1.3 mM extracellular calcium in rat hippocampal slices (Inglebert et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The DA-dependent form of plasticity described shares properties with 'late-phase' LTP, including a role of postsynaptic action potentials during induction and a requirement of protein synthesis for expression.
source: The DA-dependent form of plasticity we describe here shares properties with 'late-phase' LTP, including a role of postsynaptic action potentials during induction (Dudek and Fields, 2002) and a requirement of protein synthesis for expression (Frey et al., 1988; Huang and Kandel, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: The reactivation-induced plasticity is remarkably fast, suggesting a dissociation between different signaling pathways, rather than different temporal phases of LTP.
source: However, it is remarkably fast, suggesting a dissociation between different signaling pathways, rather than different temporal phases of LTP.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the rapid time course of the plasticity.

claim: The findings strongly support the view that the fate of a memory is not determined at the time of encoding.
source: Specifically, our findings strongly support the view that the fate of a memory is not determined at the time of encoding.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the finding that plasticity can be modulated minutes after the initial priming event.

claim: Plasticity induction can lead to two events: (1) expression of LTP or LTD, and (2) setting of a synapse-specific eligibility trace ('tagging') which allows modulation by protein synthesis-dependent signaling.
source: This is based on the finding that plasticity induction can lead to two events: (1) expression of LTP or LTD, and (2) setting of a synapse-specific eligibility trace ('tagging') which allows modulation by protein synthesis-dependent signaling.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: A major difference from the synaptic tagging hypothesis is that the findings highlight a role of DA as a key modulator of the eligibility trace.
source: A major difference is that our findings highlight a role of DA as a key modulator of the eligibility trace.
evidence: This claim is an inference comparing the current findings to the synaptic tagging hypothesis.

claim: The experimental findings uncover a synaptic learning rule that could support a two-stage model of hippocampal memory formation, in which eligibility traces are laid down during hippocampal theta activity with subsequent postsynaptic burst reactivation during sharp wave-ripples inducing LTP at those synapses.
source: Our experimental findings uncover a synaptic learning rule that could support a two-stage model of hippocampal memory formation (Buzsáki, 1989), in which eligibility traces are laid down during hippocampal theta activity with subsequent postsynaptic burst reactivation during sharp wave-ripples inducing LTP at those synapses.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the functional implications of the findings, supported by citation to the two-stage model.

claim: Substantial evidence supports a role of NMDAR-dependent STDP in the formation of place fields during navigation.
source: Substantial evidence supports a role of NMDAR-dependent STDP in the formation of place fields during navigation (Mehta, 2015; Moore et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both LTP and LTD are involved in place field formation.
source: It has been postulated that both LTP and LTD are involved in place field formation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Place fields shift backward with experience.
source: This was based on the observation that place fields shift backward with experience (Mehta et al., 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A computational model predicted that without LTD place field broadening would occur.
source: and a computational model predicted that without LTD place field broadening would occur.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling from prior work.

claim: LTP is required when entering the place field, and LTD when the animal exits the place field.
source: Thus LTP is required when entering the place field, and LTD when the animal exits the place field (Mehta et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Place field plasticity is specific to navigation, as opposed to just walking on a linear track without task.
source: This is specific to navigation, as opposed to just walking on a linear track without task
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Place field plasticity is predictive of navigational performance.
source: and place field plasticity is predictive of navigational performance (Moore et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The memory allocation hypothesis suggests that learning triggers a temporary increase in neuronal excitability, enabling the linking of individual memories acquired close in time.
source: The memory allocation hypothesis suggests that learning triggers a temporary increase in neuronal excitability, enabling the linking of individual memories acquired close in time (Silva et al., 2009; Cai et al., 2016; Sehgal et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The learning rule selectively strengthens the reactivated synapses, linking together the memory allocation hypothesis with burst reactivation-induced plasticity.
source: We found that our learning rule selectively strengthens the reactivated synapses, linking together the memory allocation hypothesis with burst reactivation-induced plasticity.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: DA released by locus coeruleus cells projecting to dCA1 has a key permissive role in contextual memory linking.
source: Interestingly, it was recently reported that DA released by locus coeruleus cells projecting to dCA1 has a key permissive role in contextual memory linking (Chowdhury et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: It is possible that DA serves as a scalar reward signal which combines with a vectorial representation of the reward identity which triggers the reactivation of a specific subset of neurons.
source: Thus, it is possible that DA serves as a scalar reward signal which combines with a vectorial representation of the reward identity which triggers the reactivation of a specific subset of neurons.
evidence: This claim is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: It was suggested that the direct pathway from the entorhinal cortex could provide an instructive signal to generate accumulation of CA1 place cells at the reward location.
source: Thus, it was suggested that the direct pathway from the entorhinal cortex could provide an instructive signal to generate accumulation of CA1 place cells at the reward location (Grienberger and Magee, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A downstream subset of neurons active during navigation could serve as an instructive input onto upstream neurons during reward.
source: An attractive possibility is that a downstream subset of neurons active during navigation serves as an instructive input onto upstream neurons during reward.
evidence: This claim is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: DA has a dual role as reinforcement signal and enhancer of reverse replay.
source: This would be consistent with a dual role of DA as reinforcement signal and enhancer of reverse replay (Ambrose et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Feedback regulation of synaptic plasticity by bursts in higher hierarchical circuits can coordinate lower-level connections.
source: It was suggested in a computational study that feedback regulation of synaptic plasticity by bursts in higher hierarchical circuits can coordinate lower-level connections (Payeur et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The results reveal a possible biological substrate to support feedback regulation of synaptic plasticity by bursts.
source: Our results reveal a possible biological substrate to support such a mechanism and re-emphasize the importance of bursting activity for synaptic plasticity (Lisman, 1997; Pike et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental results and is supported by citations to prior work on bursting.

claim: The hippocampus receives dopaminergic input from the ventral tegmental area, signaling reward.
source: The hippocampus receives dopaminergic input from two main sources, the ventral tegmental area (Scatton et al., 1980; Gasbarri et al., 1994), signaling reward
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The hippocampus receives dopaminergic input from the locus coeruleus, thought to signal novelty.
source: and the locus coeruleus (Smith and Greene, 2012; Kempadoo et al., 2016), thought to signal novelty (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Wagatsuma et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The locus coeruleus has been implicated in spatial reward learning.
source: but more recently implicated also in spatial reward learning (Kaufman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Calcium signals during locomotion were higher in CA1 principal cells that reactivated at reward location.
source: In a reward location learning task, we found that calcium signals during locomotion were higher in CA1 principal cells that reactivated at reward location.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data.

claim: The calcium signal increased in the trial preceding the first reactivation, following which the signal remained higher in all subsequent trials.
source: The signal increased in the trial preceding the first reactivation, following which the signal remained higher in all subsequent trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data.

claim: Place cells that reactivated showed higher spatial information than non-reactivating place cells in late trials.
source: Moreover, place cells that reactivated showed higher spatial information than non-reactivating place cells in late trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data.

claim: The overall stability of calcium signals and spatial information is broadly consistent with earlier reports using one-photon imaging in freely moving mice.
source: The overall stability of calcium signals and spatial information is broadly consistent with earlier reports using one-photon imaging in freely moving mice (Ziv et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Reactivation increases long-term stability of place cells that have fields distant from the reward after several days in head-fixed mice.
source: Although it was recently reported in head-fixed mice that reactivation increases long-term stability of place cells that have fields distant from the reward after several days (Grosmark et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The current study did not see a significant increase in place cell stability after a single reactivation of the cell at the reward location.
source: we did not see a significant increase in place cell stability after a single reactivation of the cell at the reward location.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data.

claim: The difference in both calcium signal and spatial information in reactivating vs non-reactivating cells is suggestive of plasticity related to reactivation events specific to reward location.
source: Irrespectively, the difference in both calcium signal and spatial information in reactivating vs non-reactivating cells is suggestive of plasticity related to reactivation events specific to reward location.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the in vivo calcium imaging results.
